title: Interference Engineering for Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution through Multiple Energy Shifts
abstract: Energy shifting is usually trivial in imaginary-time evolution because it changes only the normalization of the evolved state. On a quantum computer, however, imaginary-time evolution can be implemented as a coherent or sampled superposition of real-time evolutions, in which energy shifts generate relative phases that can interfere. Here we introduce multi-shift quantum imaginary-time evolution (MS-QITE), which uses a distribution of energy shifts to engineer interference and optimize different implementations. In a Monte Carlo realization, multi-shift reshapes the sampling distribution and concentrates it within a shorter real-time window, thereby reducing the required Hamiltonian-evolution time and improving the stability of ground-state-energy estimation. In a continuous-variable-assisted realization, it permits postselection over a finite quadrature interval rather than near a single quadrature value, substantially reducing resource consumption while retaining accurate thermal-state preparation. Numerical results for transverse-field Ising models demonstrate that energy shifts provide a useful interference-based approach for optimizing quantum imaginary-time evolution.
summary: This paper introduces Multi-shift Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution (MS-QITE) to overcome limitations in simulating quantum many-body systems on quantum computers. By engineering interference using a distribution of energy shifts, MS-QITE improves the efficiency and stability of ground-state and thermal-state preparation. This technique offers a general framework for optimizing quantum algorithms by exploiting spectral transformations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently implementing imaginary-time evolution (ITE) for ground-state and thermal-state preparation on quantum computers.
main_result: The proposed Multi-shift Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution (MS-QITE) uses a distribution of energy shifts to engineer interference, significantly improving the stability and reducing the required resources for state preparation.
method: The core method involves modifying the standard ITE by introducing a distribution of energy shifts, which transforms the evolution into a controllable real-time superposition integral.
model_or_system: The method is tested on quantum many-body systems, specifically using the transverse-field Ising model Hamiltonian. The implementation is demonstrated in both Monte Carlo sampling and continuous-variable-assisted schemes.
key_observables: Ground-state energy error, success probability, and trace distance for thermal state preparation.
important_parameters: The energy shift distribution $f(q)$, the number of shifts $k$, and the imaginary time $	au$.
main_assumptions: The approach relies on the fact that energy shifts generate relative phases that interfere when implemented on a quantum computer, even if they are trivial in normalization.
figures_summary: Figures compare probability densities with and without multi-shift, show ground-state energy error vs. cutoff time, and illustrate success probability/resource consumption for thermal state preparation.
paper_structure: The paper introduces MS-QITE by relating it to the real-time superposition of evolutions. It then details its application in Monte Carlo and continuous-variable settings, culminating in numerical results on the Ising model.
why_interesting: The technique provides a powerful, interference-based resource to optimize quantum algorithms for simulating thermal and ground states, which is a central theme in quantum simulation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Comparison of the probability densities with and without multi-shift. (b) Phase distribution over 10,000 runs with multi-shift. The parameters are a = 30, k = 3, and τ = 10.

FIG. 2. Comparison of the ground-state energy error obtained with and without multi-shift under different cutoff times tm using the function W(t) defined in Eq. (9). The results are averaged over 10 experiments. (a) Ground-state energy error with and without multi-shift for different cutoff times, with 104 Monte Carlo samples used in each experiment. (b) Ground-state energy error for different numbers of Monte Carlo samples with multi-shift for different cutoff times. The initial state is chosen to be a computational basis state. The parameters of the Ising model are n = 6, J = 2, and h = 1, with τ = 10.

FIG. 3. Illustration of the finite-photon-number approximation of the step-function state and resource state in the Fock space. As the photon-number truncation increases, the resulting state approaches the ideal state.

FIG. 4. Success probability and trace distance versus photon- number truncation for thermal-state preparation using the step-function state as the projection state. The underlying quantum Ising model has parameters n = 4, J = 1, and h = 1, and a constant has been added to ensure that all its eigenvalues are positive. The parameter L of the step- function state is chosen such that Lτ = 1.256, corresponding to the optimal success probability.
